_doc: Maps an animal name to its motion-profile body-type key (SPEC_MOTION_PROFILES §3.5) — the AI-classifier alternative to an exhaustive per-profile keyword list. A fast/Haiku call: the caller passes the animal and the LIVE registry's keys+labels as {profiles}, and the model returns the single best key. The caller (webui/motion_resolver.py) validates the returned key against the live registry and falls back to keyword resolution when the AI is unavailable or returns an unknown key — so motion_profiles stays pure data, resolution never raises, and standalone/no-key mode still works. No `enum` in the schema on purpose: the valid keys are CONTENT that changes, so they are passed in and checked caller-side, keeping this purpose registry-agnostic (adding a profile never edits this file). A CONSUMER contribution like image_triage/pet_likeness — the engine names no purpose key (§0.1/§11).
description: Classifies an animal into its body-type motion profile. The candidate keys come from the LIVE registry at call time, so this file never enumerates them — that is what lets the registry skip an exhaustive keyword list per profile.
system_prompt:
You classify an animal into ONE body-type motion category for a pet animation engine. Work in two steps.

STEP 1 — decide what the animal IS.
When the whole phrase is the established name of a real or mythical creature, the whole phrase is the animal, and you must never classify from one word of it: a `komodo dragon` is a lizard and not a dragon, a `sea horse` is a fish and not a horse, a `king cobra` is a snake, a `flying squirrel` is a squirrel that glides.
Otherwise the extra words only describe one individual — its size, age, colour, mood, or what it is covered in (hairy, furry, giant, baby, spotted). Those never change what the animal is. Strip them and classify the creature underneath: `hairy yeti` must classify exactly as `yeti`, and `giant corgi` exactly as `corgi`.

STEP 2 — classify that creature by how it MOVES: its body plan and gait — how many limbs it has, what those limbs are, and how it travels. Judge the body itself: an animal's size, colour, habitat and covering are not a body plan, and fur, feathers and scales tell you nothing about limbs. This never licenses dropping a word from the name you settled on in STEP 1 — when a creature's name contains a place, a habitat or a material, that word is part of its identity and must not be discarded as scenery.

A merely descriptive word must never change your answer. If dropping a word would change which category you pick, you have mistaken a description for a species.

Choose the single best-matching category key from the list the user gives. If nothing fits well, choose the closest body plan. Answer only in the required JSON shape.
